title: Meet Muscat
subtitle: The grape that tastes of grapes
objectives: Explain why it smells of grapes

steps.title: Grapey and floral
steps.body: Muscat is one of the few wine grapes whose wine smells of fresh grapes. Add orange blossom, rose, elderflower, peach and orange peel. Muscat wines can be dry, sweet, sparkling or fortified, from light Moscato d'Asti to rich Rutherglen Muscat. It's one of the oldest known grape families.

steps.title: Terpenes
steps.body: Muscat's aroma comes from high levels of terpenes, especially linalool, floral and citrus, and geraniol, rose. These compounds are present in the grape itself, which is why the wine smells like eating the fruit. Many Muscats are also table grapes and raisins.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Muscat its grapey, floral aroma?
steps.explanation: Terpenes, abundant in Muscat, give floral and grape aromas.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: If a wine smells exactly like fresh grapes, with orange blossom, it's almost certainly Muscat. Dry Muscat is a surprise: aromatic like a sweet wine, but dry on the palate. Compared with Gewürztraminer, Muscat is more grapey and floral, less lychee and spice.

steps.explanation: Not true. Muscat is made dry, for example in Alsace, as well as sweet and fortified.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Muscat wines smell of fresh grapes and orange blossom
Terpenes like linalool and geraniol give its aroma
It's made dry, sweet, sparkling and fortified
